title: How Not to Get Drunk at a Wedding: A Guest's Game Plan
excerpt: How to enjoy a wedding without getting too drunk: what to eat before, how to handle the cocktail hour, champagne toast and open bar, tips for the wedding party, and how to deal with a wedding hangover.
metaDescription: How not to get drunk at a wedding: eat first, pace the open bar, handle the champagne toast, and avoid a wedding-day hangover. Practical tips for guests.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the way to avoid getting drunk at a wedding is not a trick or a pill. It's a plan for the hours, because weddings are built to get people drunk by accident. You often arrive having skipped lunch, the cocktail hour hands you a drink in the first five minutes, champagne gets topped up without you asking, dinner runs late, and the open bar is free and runs for four or five hours. Most people who end up too drunk at a wedding didn't drink fast. They drank steadily for a very long time with very little food. This guide walks through each stage of the day, from the morning to the after-party, and covers what to do if you're the one getting married or you wake up the next day with a wedding hangover.

**The quick rules:** Eat a real meal with protein and fat before you leave. Start with water, not alcohol, at the cocktail hour. Hold one drink at a time and finish it before getting another. Alternate every alcoholic drink with a full glass of water. Take a small pour or skip the champagne refill before the toasts. Eat everything they put in front of you, including the bread. Stop drinking at least an hour before you plan to leave, and decide how you're getting home before you arrive.

> **When to get help right away.** Most wedding drinking ends with a rough morning, not an emergency. But if someone at the wedding can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while very drunk or semi-conscious, has cold or clammy skin with a bluish or pale tinge, or has a seizure, those are signs of alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number), stay with them, and turn them on their side so they don't choke. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to look for. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Weddings Get People Drunk Without Them Noticing

It helps to understand why weddings are so much harder than a normal night out. Once you see the traps, avoiding them is fairly easy.

- **The day is very long.** A typical wedding runs from an afternoon ceremony to a late-night reception. Even a slow pace of one drink an hour adds up to six or eight drinks over a full evening. Your body clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate, about one standard drink per hour for many adults, though it varies a lot from person to person. If you drink faster than that for hours, your blood alcohol keeps rising.
- **Food arrives late and in small amounts.** Cocktail-hour appetizers are small and easy to miss while you're talking. Dinner might not be served until two or three hours after the first drink. Alcohol absorbs much faster on an empty stomach, which is why the first hour of a wedding is often the riskiest. Our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why food slows absorption.
- **Drinks get refilled for you.** At a seated dinner, staff top up wine glasses before they're empty. You lose count because you never actually "start a new drink." Champagne for the toast lands in front of you whether you asked for it or not.
- **The bar is free.** An open bar removes the natural brake that paying provides. Nobody is counting, including you.
- **Everyone is buying rounds and making toasts.** Friends you haven't seen in years bring you a shot. A table toasts the couple. Someone says "one more" at the dance floor. The social pressure to keep a drink in your hand is high.
- **You're excited, dressed up, and often short on sleep.** Travel, nerves, and a late night before can all make alcohol hit harder than you expect.
- **Dancing and heat dehydrate you.** Packed dance floors, summer venues, and heavy formal clothes mean you're sweating, and alcohol makes you pee more on top of that.

None of these is a big deal on its own. Stacked together over six hours, they are why so many guests say "I really didn't think I drank that much."

## Before the Wedding: Set Yourself Up

The best work happens before you get there.

### Eat a real meal

This is the single most useful thing you can do. Eat a proper meal one to two hours before the ceremony, ideally with protein, fat, and some fiber: eggs, a chicken or salmon plate, a burger, a grain bowl with avocado. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol passes into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That flattens the rise in blood alcohol and gives your liver more time to keep up.

Don't count on the appetizers. If you're traveling, staying in a hotel, or getting ready with the wedding party, it's easy to skip lunch and arrive running on coffee. Pack something if you need to. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers which foods help most.

### Hydrate during the day, but don't overdo it

Drink water normally through the day so you don't start already a bit dehydrated, especially in summer or after travel. You don't need to chug liters. Just don't arrive having had nothing but coffee.

### Decide your limit and your ride now

Pick a number before the first drink, when your judgment is clear. Something like "three drinks over the evening" or "two before dinner, two after" works better than a vague "I'll take it easy." Then sort out transport ahead of time: a designated driver, a shuttle, a rideshare, or staying at the venue hotel. Having a plan for getting home takes away the temptation to "sober up" for the drive, which doesn't work fast enough to be safe.

### Get some sleep the night before

Rehearsal dinners and the night before a wedding often turn into their own party. Arriving tired and slightly hungover means less tolerance for the day ahead. If you can, cut the night before short.

## The Ceremony and Cocktail Hour: The Most Dangerous Hour

The stretch between the ceremony and dinner is where most people get ahead of themselves. You're hungry, the bar has just opened, and everyone is excited.

- **Make your first drink water or a soft drink.** Take it from the bar or a passing tray so you have something in your hand. This alone slows the first hour more than anything else.
- **Go find food.** Stand near where the appetizers come out, or ask the server what's coming. Eat several pieces, not one.
- **Choose a slower drink.** A beer, a wine spritzer, or a tall highball with lots of ice and mixer takes longer to finish than a martini or a shot. You're aiming for drinks you can sip over 45 minutes to an hour.
- **Be wary of strong signature cocktails.** Many weddings serve a custom cocktail. These can contain two or more standard drinks of liquor, and they're often sweet, so they go down quickly. If you're curious, have one and switch to something lighter.

## The Champagne Toast

The toast is a special trap because it often arrives on top of whatever you're already drinking, and the glass gets topped up afterward.

- **You don't have to drink the whole glass.** A sip is a perfectly normal way to toast. Nobody is checking.
- **Ask for a small pour or skip the refill.** Put your hand over the glass when staff come round, or leave it slightly full so it doesn't get topped up.
- **Toast with water if you'd rather.** Raising any glass is fine. Etiquette guides generally agree that toasting with a non-alcoholic drink is acceptable.

There's also a reason bubbles can feel like they hit faster. A small study from the University of Surrey found that people had higher blood alcohol levels after drinking flat versus sparkling champagne at the same strength, with the bubbly version absorbing faster in most participants. The research is limited, but it matches what many people notice. Our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) goes into more detail.

## Dinner and Wine Service: Keep Count

A seated dinner is a chance to slow down, but wine service makes it easy to lose track.

- **Eat everything.** Bread, salad, the main, dessert. This is the meal that will carry you through the rest of the night.
- **Watch the top-ups.** A wine glass that keeps getting refilled can hold far more than you think. A standard drink of wine is about 5 ounces (150 ml) at around 12% alcohol, and wedding glasses are often larger and poured generously. If you want to keep count, finish a glass before letting anyone refill it.
- **Keep a water glass next to your wine and use it.** A good rule is a full glass of water for every alcoholic drink.
- **Don't feel you have to try both the red and the white.** One glass you enjoy is better than three you didn't need.

## The Open Bar and Dancing: Pace for the Long Haul

After dinner, the bar gets busy and the dance floor opens. This is the stretch where people who were doing fine at dinner end up overdoing it.

### Use the one-drink-an-hour rule as a rough guide

Your liver works at its own pace, and nothing you do speeds it up much. A reasonable way to stay in control is to aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour, with water in between. For reference, one US standard drink is about 12 ounces of regular beer (around 5% alcohol), 5 ounces of wine (around 12%), or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits. Many wedding drinks are bigger or stronger than this, so count a large wine pour or a strong cocktail as more than one. Our guide on [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk) covers pacing in more depth.

Keep in mind that the same number of drinks affects people differently. Body size, sex, how much you've eaten, medications, and how much you usually drink all change how drunk you get. Women often reach a higher blood alcohol level than men after the same number of drinks, partly because of body water and size differences.

### Practical tricks that work at a bar

- **Hold one drink at a time.** Don't accept a new drink while you're still holding one.
- **Order singles, not doubles.** If a bartender asks "double?" the answer is no.
- **Add lots of ice and mixer.** A vodka soda or a gin and tonic in a tall glass lasts longer than the same spirit in a small one.
- **Switch to a non-alcoholic drink in a regular glass.** Soda water with lime looks exactly like a vodka soda. Many weddings now offer mocktails or non-alcoholic beer, which help you keep a drink in your hand without adding alcohol.
- **Skip shots.** Shots deliver a full standard drink in a second and stack fast. If someone hands you one, it's fine to say "I'm good" or pass it on.
- **Dance more, drink less.** Dancing is a good reason to put your drink down. Just leave it in a safe place, and get a fresh one rather than picking up a drink you lost track of.

### Watch the drink mix

You may have heard that mixing types of alcohol makes you sicker. There is no good evidence that the order or mix matters on its own. What usually happens is that switching between drinks makes it harder to count how much you've had. Darker drinks like bourbon and red wine contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation that some research links to worse hangovers than clear spirits. That doesn't change how drunk you get, but it can affect how you feel the next day.

## How to Say No Without Making It Awkward

The social side is often harder than the drinking itself. A few lines that work:

- "I'm pacing myself, it's a long night."
- "I'm good for now, thanks."
- "I've got an early start tomorrow."
- "I'm driving."
- Hold a drink you haven't touched. People rarely push a drink on someone who already has one.

Nobody at a wedding is keeping track of what you drink, and most people will forget within a minute. If someone keeps pushing, a friendly "maybe later" usually ends it.

## If You're in the Wedding Party (or Getting Married)

Bridesmaids, groomsmen, and the couple face extra pressure. You start drinking earlier, often with a mimosa or a beer while getting ready, and people want to buy you drinks all night.

### For the wedding party

- **Getting-ready drinks count.** A couple of mimosas at 11 a.m. on an empty stomach is a big head start. Have a real breakfast and order lunch for the getting-ready room.
- **You have jobs to do.** Speeches, photos, and looking after the couple all go better sober. Save the real celebrating for after your duties.
- **Give your speech before you drink much.** Nerves make people reach for a drink, but a speech given after several drinks rarely goes the way you planned.

### For the couple

- **You'll barely have time to eat.** Couples often say they hardly touched their dinner. Ask your caterer to set plates aside for you, or have someone bring you food during photos.
- **Everyone wants a drink with you.** Accept the toast, take a sip, and hand the glass back. Some couples ask the bartender to have a "couple's drink" ready that's mostly soda.
- **Remember you want to remember it.** Many couples say the day goes by in a blur even sober.

### Hungover on your wedding day

If you're worried about waking up hungover on the day itself, the answer is the night before: keep the rehearsal dinner light, stop drinking early, eat well, drink water, and go to bed at a reasonable hour. If you do wake up rough, eat a solid breakfast, drink water with some electrolytes, and rest where you can. Avoid "hair of the dog," which only pushes the hangover later into the day, when you'll be at your own reception. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the basics.

## Getting Home Safely

Decide this before you arrive and stick to it. Never drive after drinking, and don't trust feeling "fine." Coffee, cold water, and food don't lower your blood alcohol. Only time does. If the venue is remote, check the shuttle schedule, book a rideshare early, or plan to stay overnight. Keep an eye on friends too, especially anyone who slips away alone.

## The Wedding Hangover: The Morning After

If you overdid it, the next morning is about recovery, not cures. There's no fast fix, but some things help you feel better while your body catches up.

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water is the base. An electrolyte drink can help if you were sweating on the dance floor or you're also dealing with vomiting or diarrhea. Our guide on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) explains what hydration can and can't fix.
- **Eat something easy.** Toast, eggs, bananas, oatmeal, or a simple breakfast sandwich. Our list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) covers good options.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen or aspirin can irritate a stomach already upset by alcohol, so take them with food. If you use acetaminophen (Tylenol), stick to a single standard dose and don't take it on top of a heavy drinking habit.
- **Rest.** Wedding hangovers are often as much about short sleep as alcohol. Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night's sleep, so you can wake up feeling unrested even after eight hours in bed.
- **Plan the travel home carefully.** If you're driving, remember that you can still be over the limit the next morning after a heavy night. Give yourself time before getting behind the wheel.

**See a doctor if** the morning after brings vomiting you can't keep water down for many hours, confusion, severe stomach pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better as the day goes on. Those are not a normal hangover. And if you notice shaking, sweating, or anxiety that only eases when you drink again, that's worth a conversation with a doctor.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some guests take a supplement called DHM (dihydromyricetin) before or during a big event. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol and hangovers. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, and human data are limited. There is no good evidence that DHM keeps you from getting drunk, lowers your blood alcohol, or makes it safe to drink more. It won't change how alcohol affects your judgment, and it's no reason to drive or skip the pacing tips above.

If you want to try it as one part of a wedding-day plan alongside food, water, and pacing, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget pick, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing, and if you take regular medications, check with a pharmacist first. If you're putting together favors for a bachelor or bachelorette weekend before the wedding, our [bachelorette hangover kit](/never-hungover/bachelorette-hangover-kit) guide and wider [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) list practical things to include. For an honest look at which supplements are worth taking beforehand, see [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking).

## The Bottom Line

- Weddings get people drunk because they're long, food arrives late, drinks get refilled, and the bar is free.
- Eat a real meal before you go, start the cocktail hour with water, and find the appetizers.
- Sip or skip the champagne toast, watch the wine top-ups, and alternate every drink with water.
- Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour, hold one drink at a time, and skip shots.
- Plan your ride home before the first drink.
- If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, call for help and stay with them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you not get drunk at a wedding?**

Eat a full meal before you arrive, start with a non-alcoholic drink at the cocktail hour, and eat the appetizers. Hold one drink at a time, alternate each one with a glass of water, and aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour. Sip or skip the champagne toast, watch for wine refills at dinner, and avoid shots and strong signature cocktails.

**How many drinks should I have at a wedding?**

There's no single right number, because body size, sex, food, and tolerance all change how alcohol affects you. A practical approach is to set a limit in advance, such as three or four drinks spread over the evening, and keep to roughly one standard drink an hour with water in between. If you're driving, the safest number is zero.

**How do I avoid a hangover after a wedding?**

Most of the prevention happens during the wedding: eat well, pace yourself, drink water between drinks, and stop drinking an hour or more before bed. When you get home, have a glass of water and something small to eat. In the morning, rehydrate, eat a simple breakfast, and rest. There's no reliable cure, so pacing is the best tool you have.

**Is it rude to not drink at a wedding?**

No. Plenty of guests don't drink for all sorts of reasons, and nobody is keeping score. You can toast with water or a soft drink, hold a soda water with lime, or have a mocktail if one is offered. A simple "I'm pacing myself" or "I'm driving" is all the explanation anyone needs.

**Does champagne get you drunk faster?**

It may. A small study from the University of Surrey found that sparkling champagne raised blood alcohol faster than the same champagne gone flat in most participants. The evidence is limited, but it's a good reason to treat the toast as a sip rather than a full glass, especially if you haven't eaten.

**How do I avoid being hungover on my own wedding day?**

Keep the rehearsal dinner and the night before light. Stop drinking early, eat a proper meal, drink water, and get to bed at a reasonable hour. On the day, eat a real breakfast before any getting-ready drinks and make sure someone saves you a plate at the reception. If you do wake up rough, rehydrate, eat, and rest, and skip "hair of the dog."

**Does DHM stop you from getting drunk at a wedding?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol or keeps you from getting drunk. Its research is mostly in animals and lab studies, with limited human data. It doesn't change how alcohol affects your judgment or your ability to drive. If you use it, treat it as an extra alongside eating, pacing, and drinking water, not as a replacement.
